labels.name: approved

items.body:
### What problem does this PR solve?

This PR fixes correctness and memory-usage edge cases in Iceberg MVCC writes and nested schema evolution:

- An explicitly empty read could be reinterpreted as the latest snapshot after a concurrent first append. A MERGE could then miss the concurrent row and silently insert a duplicate.
- Write-schema validation used the INSERT column subset instead of the complete bind-time target schema, rejecting valid partial and static-partition INSERTs while weakening ordinal drift checks.
- Iceberg v3 row-lineage metadata columns could be mistaken for user-schema drift.
- Parent null-mask handling for nested ARRAY/MAP values could scan descendant entry maps and allocate entry-sized scratch even when the inherited mask was absent or all-clear.
- Strict cast failure semantics were incorrectly used to mark a struct field physically non-nullable even though BE narrowing casts still return `ColumnNullable`.
- Nested DESCRIBE comments were not emitted as round-trippable SQL literals.

The fix preserves the explicit empty-snapshot marker through scan planning and keeps RowDelta conflict validation anchored at table creation. In the concurrent empty-table MERGE/INSERT window, MERGE keeps reading the original empty view and its commit conflicts with the concurrent first append instead of producing duplicate data.

Write planning now carries an immutable complete target-schema snapshot separately from the write subset, validates column order, type, and Iceberg field id, and excludes engine-generated row-lineage metadata from the user-schema comparison. Nested collection alignment gates descendant scans on an inherited mask that can actually hide a row, and struct constructors preserve the physical nullability of cast results.

### Release note

Fix Iceberg empty-snapshot concurrency, partial-write schema validation, nested collection memory usage, cast-result nullability, and nested DESCRIBE comment rendering.

items.title: fix(v037): correct memory-tool-usage cross-conversation promise (F-3a)
items.body:
## Summary

**Finding F-3a** from the [v0.3.7 conversation test-findings PR plan](https://github.com/mkhomutov/Persatrix/blob/main/docs/v0.3.7-test-findings-pr-plan.md). PR 4 — the **honesty half** of F-3 (PR 5 is the substantive cross-room recall fix).

The `memory-tool-usage` snippet told every memory-capable persona *"Your memory persists across conversations."* That promise is **false** while notes are room-scoped (session = room, RFC 0031 / `memory-scope-axes.md`): a fact saved in one channel is invisible in another. Probed live, a persona that had stored a person's name said *"I don't have any notes about your name"* in a fresh channel — having promised cross-conversation memory.

## Fix

Replace the blanket promise with an honest, **current-behaviour** statement:

> Your saved notes persist over time and accumulate, but they are scoped to the conversation you are in — you may not have notes saved from a different conversation, so when recall_notes returns nothing, say so plainly rather than guess.

The "MUST call `store_note` / `recall_notes`, do not just acknowledge verbally" instruction is **preserved** — the live DB confirmed those stores land; the bug was the *scope* + the *promise*, not the tool call.

## Ordering note (deliberate)

PR 4 lands **before** PR 5 makes person-keyed recall actually cross rooms. So the wording describes **current room-scoped** behaviour and does **not** swap one false promise (*"persists across conversations"*) for another (*"remembered across rooms"*) that isn't true yet. The test even asserts `"across rooms"` is absent. **PR 5 updates this wording** when cross-room recall lands — this is the plan's "if PR 5 slips, the persona no longer over-promises" intent.

## TDD

`test_memory_tool_usage_honesty.py` written **first** — red (false promise present, honest statement absent), then snippet reworded → green (6/6). Then updated the **three other places** that pin this snippet's bytes:
- `test_persona_section_composer.py` — byte-identity golden
- `test_prompt_loader.py` — shipped-snippet byte identity
- `test_memory_instructions.py` — assertion flipped from the old promise to the honest scope

```
test_memory_tool_usage_honesty.py     6 passed
memory/prompt/persona surface      1011 passed
full unit suite                    2960 passed
```
(The 5 `TestShellExec` failures in the full run are pre-existing/environmental — bare `python` absent on PATH — identical on `main`.)

## Docs
- `docs/manual-tests/MT-PERSONA-007.md` — honest-scope live check; its Step 3 ("empty recall admitted, not guessed") is explicitly superseded by PR 5 once cross-room recall lands. Indexed in the MT README.

items.title: Correct memory usage in streaming mode using DB region sums
items.body:
## Summary
This PR adds support for correcting memory usage statistics in streaming mode by querying region sums from the database. In streaming mode, the memory locations collector uses lightweight address-only tracking, which prevents the RegionAnalyzer from computing accurate usage values from individual locations. This change reconstructs those values from aggregated data in the database.

## Key Changes
- **Added `RegionsSummary.correctedToArray()` method**: Reconstructs memory usage values using region sums from the database, combining DB data with overhead and region totals
- **Added `RegionsSummary.queryRegionSums()` static method**: Queries the `context_node_locations` table to compute SUM(size) grouped by region for a given run_id
- **Updated memory analysis commands**: Modified `MemoryCommand`, `CoreDumpReader`, and `MemoryDumpReader` to:
  - Query region sums from the database after flushing the sink
  - Use corrected summary values when region data is available
  - Fall back to original summary when no region data exists
- **Added comprehensive test coverage**: New `RegionsSummaryTest` class with tests for:
  - Corrected array generation with region sums
  - Handling empty region sums
  - Database querying with filtering (by run_id and non-null regions)
  - Unchanged behavior of the original `toArray()` method

## Implementation Details
- The correction formula adds database chunk usage + overhead + vm_stack_total + compiler_arena_total to compute corrected chunk usage
- Region sums are filtered to exclude NULL regions and only include the specified run_id
- The implementation gracefully handles missing region data by falling back to the original summary
- All three memory analysis entry points (MemoryCommand, CoreDumpReader, MemoryDumpReader) follow the same pattern for consistency

items.title: sugar-source-tree: typed enumeration over a query backend, replacing the node membrane (#5940)
items.body: Part of #5940. Does not close #5940. ## Shape Strongly typed objects enumerating strongly typed children, delegating to a swappable backend: - `SourceTree` — literally a glob: `rglob("*.py")`, skip `__pycache__`, yield a typed `SourceFile` per path. Nothing else. - `SourceFile(filename, source, backend)` — parses at construction; `nodes()` enumerates every node; holding its tree IS the file, not a cache. - `Node` — every accessor (`Call.args`, `Call.receiver()`, `FunctionDef.body`, `Name.id`) is a QUERY answered by the backend at access time. Arity lives in the class annotations. An accessor the backend cannot answer panics loudly, naming the accessor. The node classes are the contract. `Backend.root(unit)` answers the file-level query; `BackendNode.describe()` answers the per-node children query; backend-internal retention is the adapter's own affair, below the line. Our layer holds nothing between calls: no pool, no keyed store, no memo, no stamping. ## Kept / discarded (replaced `sugar-node-membrane` in place, renamed) Kept whole: ~80 node classes, `Typeable`/`Typed`, operators as classes, both panic types (`VocabularyMissing` / `BackendDefect`, ex `MembraneMissing`/`MembraneProviderDefect`), the refusal type (`BackendRefused`, ex `ProviderRefused`), the span module, all four adapters. `sugar-typed-recognition` untouched. Discarded: `parse(source) -> whole tree` entry point, `NodePool` + all interning, the eager bottom-up builder (`construct.py`), the membrane naming. ## Corpus: numpy+pandas, 1,828 files (battleaxe, bench-venv 3.12) | backend | files | nodes | panics | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---|---| | cpython-ast | 1828/1828 | 2,947,219 | 0 | 104 MiB, flat from first checkpoint | | tree-sitter-python | 1828/1828 | 2,831,506 | 0 | 104 MiB, flat | | libcst | 1828/1828 | 2,948,123 | 0 | 420 MiB, flat | | parso | ~1372 clean | ~1.95M | ~106 | 52 MiB, flat | RSS checkpoints every 200 files are byte-identical from file 200 to file 1800 on all backends: peak RSS does not grow with corpus size. 81 tests pass on battleaxe. ## Drained along the way - Pre-existing broken import: parso and tree-sitter adapters imported a nonexistent `membrane_panic` (now `vocabulary_missing`). - PEP 696 `default_value` added to `TypeVar`/`ParamSpec`/`TypeVarTuple`. - tree-sitter 17 -> 0 panics: `tuple_pattern`/`list_splat_pattern` targets, `with (X as a)` parenthesized items, PEP 695 `constrained_type` on type aliases, bare-tuple expression statements, `line_continuation` in comparisons. - parso 202 crashes -> 0: `x: T = v` (annassign) hit `op.value` on a node; `root()` raised `SyntaxError` instead of `BackendRefused` (contract violation). ## Findings - **parso remaining gaps** (named, not worked around): f-string format-spec family (~63 panics), chained `for ... for ...` comprehension folds (~26), `**` leaf (~2); `match` statements refuse (parso's shipped grammar has no match productions). - **Box-level segfault on battleaxe**: nondeterministic interpreter-level segv (IP inside python3.12, dmesg confirms) during long corpus runs, reproducible with **bare parso and zero sugar code loaded**; also corrupts parso's DFA tables mid-process (332 `DFAState` AttributeErrors in one chunk). This is the segv lanes' known battleaxe issue, not this package. ## Summary
- Removes `local item_lag_preventer = table.length(res.items)` from `battlemod/statics.lua`
- This line forces the entire Windower `res.items` table to materialize in memory (~20MB) but the variable is never referenced anywhere in the codebase
- Saves ~20MB RAM per client, ~120MB+ for multiboxers running 6+ instances

## Details
`table.length(res.items)` iterates every item in the FFXI item database to produce a count. The count is stored in a local that is never read. Meanwhile, the iteration forces Windower's lazy-loading resource system to fully materialize all item entries into memory.

Benchmarked cold `res.items[id]` lookups at ~0.2ms per access. BattleMod only accesses `res.items` for infrequent item drop messages, so lazy loading has no perceptible impact on gameplay.

- Memory usage drops from ~28MB to ~2MB idle

items.title: fix(observability): close two selector blind spots in check_alert_series.py
items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #855. cAdvisor emits zero Docker container series because the host's containerd-snapshotter storage driver has no overlayfs layerdb — so `container_memory_usage_bytes` exists (40 series) but never carries a `name` label. That raised the natural next question: **can `check_alert_series.py` see this shape at all** — a rule matching a live *metric* but a dead *label value*? It could not, for two separate reasons, each proven against live production Prometheus with a synthetic rule before either fix was written.

### Blind spot 1 — `absent()`/`absent_over_time()` inversion
A selector that is the direct argument of `absent(...)` was checked with the same "0 series = broken rule" logic as every other selector. That's backwards for this one construct — 0 series is exactly the designed firing condition. Six real rules in `alerts.yml` use this shape (`LokiIngestionStalled`/`SignalMissing`, `BackupNotSucceeding*`, `ScheduledWorkflow*`); four of the six only "passed" before this fix because the underlying metric happens to have series right now. The moment one genuinely went absent, the old code would report the rule as broken — exactly backwards at the one moment it matters.

### Blind spot 2 — grouping/join/annotation labels invisible to extraction
A label referenced only via `by()`/`without()`/`on()`/`ignoring()`/`group_left()`/`group_right()`, or only inside a `{{ $labels.x }}` annotation template, was never seen: `STRIP` deletes the grouping clause's contents before metric names are matched, and annotations are a separate YAML field `selectors_in()` never reads. This is the historical `HighMemoryUsage` shape (fixed by renaming to `HostMemoryHigh`, per the file's own docstring), reached through aggregation instead of an explicit `{name="x"}` matcher — and the check script's blind spot to that *shape* was never closed.

## Proof (before/after, live production Prometheus, three synthetic rules)

| Rule | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `PROOF_AbsentInversion` (`absent(fake_metric)`) | **incorrectly failed** — "0 SERIES — this rule cannot fire" | correctly reported as `~` (firing condition, not a failure) |
| `PROOF_ByGroupingHidesLabel` (`sum by (name) (container_memory_usage_bytes)`) | **incorrectly passed** — "ok 40 series" | correctly caught — `NO container_memory_usage_bytes{name!=""} 0 SERIES` |
| `PROOF_GenuinelyHealthyGrouping` (`sum by (mountpoint) (node_filesystem_avail_bytes)`, negative control) | n/a | passes both base and synthetic checks — proves the fix discriminates rather than failing every grouping clause |

Then re-ran the fixed script against the **real** `alerts.yml` on the VPS: 55 selectors checked (up from 34, from the new synthetic checks), **exit 0, no regressions** — all six real `absent()`-wrapped rules behave correctly, no existing grouping/annotation label produces a new false positive, and stale-allowlist detection is unchanged (an allowlisted selector with real series is still reported STALE before the absent-exemption branch is reached).

Read-only throughout: instant Prometheus queries only, nothing enabled/written/restarted.

items.body:
💡 What:
Replaced O(N) `queue.shift()` operations with a fast `queue[head++]` pointer in the BFS traversal functions in `src/kinship/calculator.ts`. Additionally, moved the dynamic filtering/sorting of adjacency lists out of the hot traversal loop and into the `buildAdjacency` initialization step.

🎯 Why:
The kinship calculator performs multiple BFS traversals on the graph. `Array.shift()` in JavaScript is an O(N) operation. Executing it inside the traversal loop changes the BFS time complexity from O(V + E) to O(V^2), which significantly degrades performance on larger family trees. Additionally, re-filtering the adjacency list (`...neighbors.filter(...)`) for every single node visited created immense memory allocation and garbage collection pressure.

📊 Impact:
- Transforms BFS dequeue complexity from O(N) to O(1).
- Eliminates repeated array creation and filtering during traversal, reducing garbage collection pressure.
- Overall calculation should be noticeably faster on large family trees.

Run `npm run test` to verify calculations remain correct, and observe reduced CPU and memory usage when calculating kinships in large trees.

## Summary

Implements streaming PDF export to prevent memory exhaustion when exporting large violation datasets. Processes violations in configurable batches instead of loading everything into memory at once.

## Problem

Currently PDF export loads all violations into memory:
- Memory exhaustion with thousands of reports
- Timeout errors on large exports
- Slow performance during generation
- Unresponsive UI during export
- System slowdowns from memory pressure

## Solution

Created StreamingPDFExporter with batch processing:
- Processes violations in configurable batches (default 100)
- Progress callbacks for user feedback
- Efficient memory management with event loop yielding
- Filtering support (status, type, date range)
- Summary statistics generation
- Severity-based highlighting
- Memory estimation and optimization
- Direct download capability

## Changes

- New `src/lib/pdf-exporter.ts` module
- StreamingPDFExporter class with batch processing
- generatePDFBlob() for blob generation
- generateAndDownload() for direct downloads
- Memory estimation and batch size optimization
- Progress tracking callbacks
- Filtering and summary capabilities

## Technical Details

Streaming approach:
1. Filters violations based on criteria
2. Processes violations in batches of 100 (configurable)
3. Generates PDF content incrementally
4. Yields control to event loop between batches
5. Calls progress callback for UI updates
6. Collects chunks into final blob
7. Triggers download when complete

Batch Processing Benefits:
- Linear memory usage regardless of dataset size
- Responsive UI with progress updates
- Prevention of timeout errors
- Graceful degradation on slow systems
- Ability to handle millions of records

## Testing Strategy

- Export small datasets (< 100 records)

- Export large datasets (1000-10000 records)
- Test filtering with large datasets
- Verify progress callbacks fire correctly
- Test memory usage during export
- Test download functionality

items.body:
## What

This PR swaps Linux linking from GNU ld over to LLD. It is faster and less memory hungry.

## Measurement

pg_search links datafusion, arrow and tantivy into one cdylib, so the link is large. I captured the exact `cc` argv rustc invokes for `libpg_search.so` and replayed it under each linker, so this is the real link rather than a full rebuild with the delta inferred out of it.

linux/arm64, 8 cores, matching the CI runner shape. Debug cdylib, three runs each:

| linker | run 1 | run 2 | run 3 | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GNU ld | 40.3s | 31.3s | 37.7s | 3.78 GB |
| LLD | 10.5s | 10.8s | 9.5s | 3.50 GB |

**~3.5x faster, roughly 26s back per link.** Every job that runs `cargo pgrx install` pays this, and the coverage jobs pay it more than once. Peak memory usage is ~7% lower.

## Correctness

Both linkers export an identical set of **1639** dynamic symbols, and both emit `Pg_magic_func`, so pgrx's `--version-script` and `--no-undefined-version` are honoured the same way by each. LLD's output is ~2% larger (813 MB vs 796 MB, debug).

### 💡 What
This pull request replaces `Option<PathBuf>` with `Option<Arc<PathBuf>>` within the memoization caches of `HeaderSearch` (`resolve_cache` and `resolve_next_cache`). 

### 🎯 Why
Previously, even if a path lookup was cached, every cache hit cloned the `PathBuf`. Because `PathBuf` owns its heap-allocated string representation, this resulted in continuous heap allocations and deep copying of the path string on every `#include` directive query—which is a major bottleneck when compiling large codebases such as SQLite (with thousands of nested includes).

### 📊 Impact
* **Completely eliminates heap allocations and string copies** on cached header resolution queries (which represent ~99% of include lookups).
* Retains exact logical correctness and safety.
* Yields measurable speedup and lower memory usage for preprocessor-heavy workloads.

### 🔬 Measurement
All 1550+ unit tests pass, and statistical benchmarks can be verified by running `cargo bench --bench compiler_benches`.

items.title: fix(clickhouse): load profile settings via users.d in customConfig
items.body:
## Problem
`customConfig` in the ClickHouse chart was mounted **only** into `/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/`. ClickHouse reads **server-level** settings from `config.d`, but **profile/user** settings are read **only** from the users config tree (`users.d`). So a `<profiles>` block placed in `customConfig` was **silently ignored** — no error, no warning, just no effect.

Observed live on the `zopnight` release: `max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio` (server-level) applied correctly, but `max_memory_usage`, `max_bytes_before_external_group_by`, and `max_bytes_before_external_sort` (profile-level) never loaded (`changed=0`, `default` profile empty). This contributed to ClickHouse OOMs (code 241) on heavy aggregation queries, since the intended per-query cap and spill-to-disk thresholds were never in effect.

This is standard ClickHouse behavior on the **official image** (not a Bitnami/chart quirk) — `config.d` and `users.d` are separate trees read by different parts of the server.

## Fix
Mount the same `customConfig` document into **both** trees:
- `/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/custom.xml` — server-level settings
- `/etc/clickhouse-server/users.d/custom.xml` — profile/user settings

ClickHouse reads the relevant sections from each tree and ignores the rest, so a single document can carry both. **No change to deploy values is required** — existing `customConfig` blobs start working after a `helm upgrade`.

## Verification (minikube, official `clickhouse/clickhouse-server:25.3`)
- Render: empty `customConfig` → no ConfigMap/mounts; server-only / profiles-only / mixed → both mounts render.
- Live deploy of the real mixed config:
  - Pod `Running 1/1`, **0 restarts**; no config-related errors/warnings in logs.
  - Server setting `max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio=0.9` → `changed=1`.
  - Profile settings `max_memory_usage=1.5G`, `max_bytes_before_external_group_by=750M`, `max_bytes_before_external_sort=750M` → all `changed=1`; `default` profile populated; enforced via `getSetting()`.
  - **Non-default users**: created `aggregator_tpbh` exactly as the chart does (SQL `CREATE USER`, no settings profile) and confirmed it inherits all three limits via the server `default_profile`.

## Changes
- `templates/statefulset.yaml` — add `users.d/custom.xml` mount of the existing `custom-config` ConfigMap.
- `values.yaml` — document both mount paths in the `customConfig` comment.
- `README.md` — document dual-mount behavior with example.

items.title: Clean up expired per-IP entries in `IpRateLimiter`
items.body:
Hey, awesome project! I've been working on my own `ratatui` + `russh` app recently, so I was excited to dig into this.

While reading through the rate limiter, I noticed that expired per-IP entries can stick around indefinitely in the `HashMap`, which means scanner traffic can accumulate in the map until restart. This PR adds a periodic cleanup to remove those expired entries.

## Problem

`IpRateLimiter::allow()` prunes expired timestamps from the current IP's `VecDeque`, but it does not remove the IP key from the outer `HashMap` when that deque becomes empty.

That means IPs that hit the limiter once and never call `allow()` again can leave behind empty map entries indefinitely. For an internet-facing service, scanner traffic can make that map grow monotonically until restart.

## Impact

- Rate-limiting behavior is unchanged. Empty entries do not affect correctness.
- Memory usage can grow without bound as new source IPs accumulate.
- Both `ssh_attempt_limiter` and `ws_pair_limiter` are affected.

## Fix

Add a periodic background cleanup task that sweeps each limiter's `attempts_by_ip` map, removes expired timestamps, and drops IP entries whose queues become empty.

This keeps the `O(n)` sweep off the request path. Expired entries may remain until the next cleanup tick, but map growth is bounded instead of unbounded.

## Verification

- Added a unit test that confirms cleanup removes an IP entry after its timestamps expire.
- Added a unit test that confirms cleanup preserves IPs with active timestamps.

The original implementation **only calculated `blocks_needed` based on the first KV-Cache group (index `0`)**. 📌 Description

This PR fixes a resource-exhaustion vulnerability in api/routes/document_verification.py:30,41 where user-supplied Base64 content was decoded without validating the decoded output size.

Previously, the document verification workflow processed arbitrary payloads using:

base64.b64decode(req.file_base64)

without enforcing limits on the resulting decoded data size.

Current behavior before the fix:

Arbitrary Base64 payload sizes were accepted
No decoded-size validation existed before memory allocation
Pydantic validation checked only input type (str)
Extremely large payloads could be decoded directly into memory
File-processing endpoints lacked resource exhaustion protections

Because Base64 decoding expands attacker-controlled input into raw binary data, malicious users could submit oversized payloads that decode into gigabytes of memory consumption.

As a result:

Memory exhaustion attacks became possible
Application processes could crash due to OOM conditions
Service availability could be disrupted
Resource exhaustion denial-of-service attacks became feasible
Large decode operations could destabilize the server

The updated implementation introduces strict validation and size enforcement before Base64 decoding occurs.

With these changes:

Base64 payloads are validated against strict size limits
Oversized decoded content is rejected safely before allocation
Memory usage protections are enforced for document-processing endpoints
Resource exhaustion attack vectors are significantly reduced
File upload handling becomes safer and more predictable

items.title: MQE: support CSE on range vectors in range queries
items.body:
#### What this PR does

This PR extends the CSE/SSE optimisation pass and range vector operator to support CSE/SSE on range vectors in range queries.

Previously, CSE/SSE was only supported if the range vector was evaluated in an instant query.

This implementation builds upon the existing optimisation pass and operator, storing each step's samples in a separate slice in the `rangeVectorSeriesDataRingBuffer`. 

This approach is fine for queries where the ranges of each step do not overlap (eg. `foo[2m]` in a range query with a 5m step), but for queries where the ranges of each step do overlap (eg. `foo[2m]` in a range query with a 1m step), the samples in the overlapping area will be stored separately multiple times. A future improvement would be to use one `types.FPointRingBuffer` and `types.HPointRingBuffer` for each buffered series, only appending previously-unseen samples to the buffer, but I've chosen to omit that here in the interests of keeping this PR manageable.

items.body: ## 🛠️ Description of Changes This PR resolves a critical memory exhaustion and Denial-of-Service (DoS) vulnerability within the Batch Triage workflow in `app.py`. Previously, the Streamlit dashboard accepted arbitrary CSV uploads and immediately materialized the entire file into a `pandas` DataFrame. It then iterated through the rows to post synchronous fraud-check requests. Without a file-size gate, row cap, or backpressure mechanism, a maliciously crafted or oversized CSV could easily exhaust the server's session memory, lock up the UI thread, and hammer the backend API with unconstrained traffic. I refactored the CSV upload and processing pipeline to be strictly bounded and memory-safe: 1. **File-Size Gating:** Introduced `MAX_BATCH_UPLOAD_BYTES`. The app now processes and frees memory in strict chunks. 3. **Hard Row Caps:** Introduced `BATCH_MAX_ROWS` to automatically halt processing if a file exceeds the maximum allowed batch depth. 4. **Edge Case Handling:** Added a guard to ensure empty CSVs fail gracefully instead of falling through into empty analytics or dividing by zero. `MemoryTrackingMiddleware` uses `memory_get_usage(true)` for its leak-detection warning, which returns OS-level page allocation. items.title: fix(api): stream the Wordfence Production feed + 8m fetch budget (GH #245 follow-up) — 0.61.74
items.body:
Post-deploy verification of 0.61.73 exposed the *real* reason CVSS still wasn't landing. With the wall-clock spacing fix, a Production request reached Wordfence cleanly **for the first time ever** (it always 429'd before), and the actual large-feed download surfaced two latent bugs the rate-limiting had masked:

1. **OOM.** Prod logged `Container terminated on signal 9` (SIGKILL) 10s into the fetch. The Production feed is the full enriched dataset (CVSS/CVE/CWE/references per vuln) vs Scanner's ~37k minimal records; every record was accumulated into one whole-feed map, blowing past the 1Gi instance.
2. **Timeout-in-waiting.** The fetch shared the 30s `http.Client.Timeout` meant for agent-update traffic. Pre-fix it OOM'd before 30s; once streaming stops the OOM, the full download exceeds 30s and would hit that timeout. Fixed before it could bite.

### Fix (CP-only, no schema change)
- **Stream the Production ingest** — token-stream the JSON and flush to the DB in bounded batches of 500 (each its own tx, so a mid-stream failure keeps prior batches). Batch slice reused (`batch[:0]`) → memory O(batch), never O(feed). Scanner left buffered/unchanged (it fits + owns prune).

## #15 — retry backoff
The per-attempt backoff after a non-retryable/empty failure was `time.sleep(min(2 ** attempt * 2, 30))`. Doubled to `min(2 ** attempt * 4, 30)` so attempts space out more under provider pressure; the 30s cap is unchanged so a worker is never blocked for minutes.

The original PR-B also reversed cost for provider-glitch (`finish_reason=null`) empty responses. Making it consistent requires deciding whether `finish_reason=null` responses are billed by the provider at all — a budget-semantics call left to the maintainer (tracked in the repo's bug handoff, alongside the finish_reason classification question). So this PR is scoped to the safe backoff change only.

`tests/test_llm_budget.py` asserts the backoff is `2**attempt*4` capped at 30.

Both ClickHouse replicas refuse to start:

```
Code: 36. DB::Exception: The value of 'number_of_free_entries_in_pool_to_execute_mutation'
setting (20) is greater than 'background_pool_size' *
'background_merges_mutations_concurrency_ratio' (16). (BAD_ARGUMENTS)
```

I set `background_pool_size: 8` to cap merge memory, but ClickHouse sanity-checks it against the mutation pool — with defaults (ratio 2, 20 entries) anything under 10 fails outright and the server exits before listening. Pods showed `Running 0/1` with the startup probe getting connection refused on 8123, and `otel-ingest` crash-looped behind them.

Raised to 16 (upstream default). Merge memory is bounded by `max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio`, which is the correct lever — pool size is a concurrency setting, not a memory one.

items.title: fix(buffer): avoid full content undo patch materialization
items.body:
# TL;DR
Undo history now records small byte-range patches without flattening whole documents during patch construction. This keeps the existing `Document` + `EditDelta` + `UndoPatch` model, but adds gap-aware byte queries so undo can capture only the changed bytes.

Closes #1889

## Context
Issue #1889 identified that undo patch construction was still materializing full buffer content, even when an edit delta already identified the changed byte range. That made large-file edits allocate work proportional to file size instead of edit size.

This PR keeps the architecture vocabulary narrow: `Document` owns efficient access to gap-buffer storage, `EditDelta` describes the change, and `UndoPatch` derives the reversible patch from the delta plus the old document.

## Changes
- Added gap-aware `Document.content_byte_size/1`, `Document.byte_at/2`, and `Document.slice_byte_range/3` queries.
- Reworked `UndoPatch.from_delta/2` and `UndoPatch.from_documents/2` so patch construction no longer calls `Document.content/1`.
- Copied captured patch binaries with `:binary.copy/1` so small undo patches do not retain large source document binaries through sub-binary references.
- Changed find-and-replace undo recording to use delta-backed patches instead of forced full-document diff patches.
- Reworked line deletion and clear-line delta construction through `Minga.Buffer.Operation` instead of full old/new document content diffing.
- Moved batch replacement patch sequencing into `Minga.Buffer.Replace`, keeping replacement semantics out of the GenServer orchestration layer.
- Added regression coverage for gap-crossing slices, patch binary ownership, redo round trips, clear-line undo/redo, and the 1000-entry large-file memory target.

## Verification
- `mix test.llm test/minga/buffer/document_test.exs test/minga/buffer/undo_patch_test.exs test/minga/buffer/process_test.exs test/minga/buffer/operation_test.exs test/minga/buffer/replace_test.exs test/minga/buffer/delete_lines_test.exs test/minga/buffer/undo_test.exs` ✅
- `mix test.llm test/minga/buffer` ✅, 621 tests
- `make lint` ✅
- `mix test.llm` ✅, 8698 tests, 0 failures, 268 excluded
- Parent-orchestrated review loop: 2 rounds, final Round 2 PASS from correctness, test, and simplicity reviewers

## Acceptance Criteria Addressed
- No undo-related code path calls `Document.content/1` for patch computation ✅
- Undo patches are constructed from edit deltas or direct mutation context ✅
- Undo/redo behavior is unchanged, existing undo tests pass ✅
- Coalescing of rapid edits still works correctly ✅
- Memory usage for 1000 undo entries on a 1 MB file stays under 10 MB ✅

items.title: Recover Codex token counts for backfill and normalize token usage: net input + one carrier row per response
items.body:
Makes `attributes.usage` on `ai_gateway_messages` analyzable without
  provider/capture-mode special-casing, and recovers Codex token counts for
  backfill. Motivated by an analyst hitting a silent ~2.5× overcount and the
  wrong storage path. New design doc: **LLP 0035**; revises **LLP 0026**.

  ## What & why

  Token usage was a confidently-wrong-numbers trap:
  - `usage.input_tokens` meant *uncached* input for Claude but *cache-inclusive*
    for Codex — same column, two meanings.
  - Claude duplicated the response-level `usage` onto **every** content-block row,
    so a naive `SUM` over-counted ~2.5×; Codex put it on one row → inconsistent.
  - The documented recipe read `raw_frame.message.usage`, which is null for
    Claude *live* and all Codex (only Claude backfill has the raw frame, under the
    flat `raw_frame.message_id`).

  Two invariants fix it (LLP 0035):

  1. **Net input, everywhere.** `input_tokens` is uncached for both providers;
     cache rides `cache_read_tokens` (`+ cache_write_tokens` for Claude). So
     `input + cache_read [+ cache_write] = total prompt` dataset-wide, and
     `input + cache_read + output == total_tokens` reconciles.
  2. **One carrier per response, on the last assistant row** — the terminal
     output item (`tool_use`, else final `text`), the same row as `stop_reason`.
     A plain `SUM(attributes.usage.*)` is now correct, and Claude and Codex render
     identically in the table.

  ## Changes

  **Codex backfill** — recover per-turn usage from `token_count` rollout events
  (`last_token_usage`, never the cumulative `total_token_usage`); net-input
  normalization; stamp on the turn's last assistant row.

  **Codex live** (`exchange-projector.js`) — net-input normalization; usage on the
  last assistant message (`stampUsageOnLastAssistant`).

  **Claude live + backfill** — stamp response-level `usage` once, on the last
  block of each API message (alongside `stop_reason`), instead of every block.

  **Gateway** (`message_projector.js`) — `expandMessageParts` stamps `usage` on
  only the last part of a multi-block message (`stripUsage`), making the
  one-carrier rule structural. (Claude backfill does emit multi-block carrier
  messages — `reasoning + text`, `reasoning + tool_use`, parallel tool calls —
  which were the only rows a plain `SUM` over-counted.)

  **Docs / memory** — new LLP 0035 (incl. the canonical `attributes.usage` query);
  LLP 0026 consequence revised; the `reference-token-accounting-method` memory
  corrected (`attributes.usage`, not `raw_frame`).

  ## Compatibility

  No in-app consumer reads `attributes.usage` — verified across context graph,
  enrichment, sinks, datasets, and vector search; it's only ad-hoc/skill SQL.
  The `max()`-per-`COALESCE(raw_frame.message_id, message_id)` rollup still works
  on both old (duplicated) and new (single-carrier) data.

items.title: Fix SM utilization reporting for forked CUDA worker processes
items.body:
## Problem

  For Python multiprocessing workloads using HAMi-core, `Device_utilization_desc_of_container` may stay at 0 even when GPU processes are actively running.

  In the affected workload:

  - `nvidia-smi pmon` inside the container reports ~97% SM utilization per worker process.
  - `nvmlDeviceGetProcessUtilization` inside the container returns correct per-process samples.
  - `vGPU_device_memory_usage_in_bytes` is updated correctly.
  - `Device_utilization_desc_of_container` remains 0.
  - The shared cache has valid memory usage and updated `last_kernel_time`, but `device_util[].sm_util` stays 0.

  ## Root Cause

  `postInit()` starts the utilization watcher via `init_utilization_watcher()`, but it is guarded by `pthread_once(post_cuinit_flag)` and is only reliably triggered through the
`cuInit()` wrapper.

  For forked Python multiprocessing workers, the child process may inherit a completed `post_cuinit_flag` from the parent. Later CUDA kernel launches in the worker call the hooked launch path, but `postInit()` is skipped, so host PID detection and utilization watcher initialization never happen in the worker process.

  There is also an existing multi-GPU bug in `init_gpu_device_utilization()`: the inner loop breaks after device 0, so only the first device is reset. See[#148 ](https://github.com/Project-HAMi/HAMi-core/issues/148)

  ## Fix

  - Add `ensure_post_init()` and call it from kernel launch wrappers.
  - Reset `post_cuinit_flag` and `pidfound` in the child process after fork.
  - Remove the erroneous `break` in `init_gpu_device_utilization()`.

  ## Validation

  Tested with an 8-GPU Python multiprocessing workload:

  Before:

  - `nvidia-smi pmon`: ~97% SM utilization
  - `Device_utilization_desc_of_container`: 0

  After:

  - `Device_utilization_desc_of_container`: 97-98 per GPU
  - vGPU memory metrics remain correct

items.title: fix(worker): configurable build timeout with clean abort (#33)
items.body:
## Summary

Addresses #33 (resource management during the screenshot process). Adds a configurable per-build wall-clock timeout to the worker so a stuck or pathologically large Storybook build can no longer pin the worker indefinitely, plus per-build memory-usage logging for observability.

Previously the only backstop was `sweepStuckBuilds()`, which marks a build failed only after **2 hours** of `running` — and only when the worker is *idle*, so a genuinely hung build never reached it.

## Changes

- **`worker/src/timeout.ts` (new):** `BuildTimeoutError` + `withTimeout(work, ms, onTimeout)` helper.
- **`worker/src/environment.ts`:** `BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 15 min) and `BUILD_MEMORY_WARN_BYTES` (default 2 GiB), both env-configurable.
- **`worker/src/ingest.ts`:** render phase wrapped in `withTimeout`; on timeout the browser session is force-closed (interrupting in-flight WebDriver commands so the stack unwinds and existing `finally` cleanup runs), the `ScreenshotTest` is marked `failed`, and VCS status is updated. Adds `logBuildMemoryUsage` (RSS/heap at render start/end, `warn` past threshold) and guards teardown `deleteSession()` so a double-close can't mask the original error.
- **`worker/src/worker.ts` (`processTask`):** a `BuildTimeoutError` is **non-retryable** — the task is deleted from the queue rather than having its lock released for backoff retry. All other errors keep the existing release-and-retry behavior.

## Design decisions

- **15 min default:** generous for healthy large builds, well under the 2-hour stuck-sweep so the worker recovers promptly.
- **Non-retryable timeout:** retrying a stuck/huge build just burns another full window; the build is already marked failed.
- **Abort via `deleteSession()`:** the work promise isn't independently cancellable, so closing the browser is what interrupts it.

## Done vs deferred

- **Done:** build timeout (configurable, clean abort, correct task disposition) + memory-usage logging/warning + tests.
- **Deferred:** periodic service restart (max-builds-then-exit counter) — plan documented in #33. Deferred because the timeout removes the acute risk, it needs a graceful-drain handshake with the poll loop / health server, and the right N is best chosen after the new memory logs accumulate.

## Validation (Node 26)

`yarn build:all`, `yarn lint:all`, `yarn test:all` all pass; `yarn dedupe --check` clean. New tests: `worker/src/timeout.test.ts` and a timeout-abort case in `worker/src/worker.test.ts` (asserts `BuildTimeoutError` + `status: "failed"`).

items.title: fix(drivers: pwm): fix GPT_CCMRX macro unaligned access for ch 2/3
items.body:
The GPT_CCMRX(ch) macro computes the CCMR register byte offset as:
  GPT_CCMR1 + (ch >> 1)

For channels 2 and 3 this yields GPT_CCMR1 + 1, which is an odd (unaligned) address. Subsequent 32-bit read/write via sys_clear_bits() / sys_set_bits() on that address triggers a CPU usage fault (Unaligned memory access).

The correct offset for CCMR2 is GPT_CCMR1 + 4 (one 32-bit word after CCMR1). Fix the macro by shifting left by 2 after the divide, matching the pattern already used by the CCRX(ch) macro.

Fixes crash when using GPTIM2 PWM channels 2 or 3.

I have implemented several performance optimizations in the backend API handlers to reduce database roundtrips and memory overhead.

### Key Changes:
- **Consolidated Stats Queries**: Refactored `GetLibraryStats` and `GetSummary` in `stats.go` to merge multiple sequential count/sum operations into unified queries (using JOINs or subqueries). This reduces the number of database roundtrips for the most prominent dashboard metrics.
- **Targeted Column Selection**: Applied targeted `.Select()` clauses to `RenderLibrariesPartial`, `WatchlistHandler.GetForm`, `SchedulesHandler.GetForm`, and `ArtistsHandler.GetForm`. By fetching only necessary identification fields (`id`, `name`) for dropdowns and lists, we reduce database I/O and memory allocation.
- **BOLA Correction**: Improved the QualityProfile count in the summary view to correctly include system default profiles for non-administrator users, ensuring consistency with the actual profile selection logic.

### Impact:
- `GetLibraryStats`: Reduced DB roundtrips from 4 to 2.
- `GetSummary`: Reduced DB roundtrips from 3 to 2.
- `GetForm` Handlers: Reduced memory overhead and I/O by avoiding full model scans for simple dropdown populations.

All changes were verified with integration tests and visual inspection of server logs and frontend components.

items.title: perf: share call-local Vulkan resources
items.body:
## Summary
- reuse exact guest-buffer uploads, image-view/sampler pairs, descriptor-set layouts, and pipeline layouts within one Vulkan submission
- allocate one descriptor pool per submission instead of one per draw while retaining fence-before-destroy lifetime safety
- preserve resource identity and complete immutable view/sampler contracts; zero/synthetic identities and distinct guest allocations never alias
- remove the reintroduced independent-review mandate from `CLAUDE.md`, as previously requested, to avoid mandatory duplicate subscription/token usage
- correct the Windows direct-memory/write-watch documentation after the red-zone correctness fix in #944

Progress on #702.

## Evergate profile

A matched late-title/intro window improved as follows:

| metric | keyed sharing disabled | call-local sharing |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| draws | 475.2 | 472.0 |
| whole submit | 409.1 ms | 354.1 ms |
| backend | 285.8 ms | 218.7 ms |
| resource setup | 84.0 ms | 64.6 ms |
| pipeline-layout work | 16.9 ms | 2.0 ms |
| cleanup | 103.4 ms | 72.7 ms |
| observed app rate | ~2.4 FPS | ~2.7 FPS |

A broader index/descriptor-bundle reuse experiment regressed the same window to about 483.9 ms and was removed rather than included.

## Correctness contract
- storage buffers share only for the same nonzero guest identity, exact size, hash, and bytes
- texture view/sampler reuse is keyed by the underlying image plus the complete immutable view/sampler configuration
- descriptor and pipeline layouts share only for exact structural equality
- all call-local Vulkan objects are destroyed after the existing fence wait
- `PROSPER_NO_BACKEND_RESOURCE_SHARE=1` provides the keyed-reuse A/B control

## Verification
Exact head `b9635011137dcfaf43422bf4b56bb5d851711350`:
- repository renderer author verification: PASS
- Linux build + 110/110 tests: PASS
- Windows build + 85/85 tests: PASS
- `evergate-title` animated snapshot: PASS (9/9 qualifying, structural, and non-black frames)
- focused renderer tests assert identical output with reuse enabled and disabled, plus non-aliasing for distinct guest identities and distinct texture swizzles

This patch changes resource construction and lifetime only; rendered pixels remain byte-identical, so it does not update the approved screenshot baseline.

items.title: Scope cache to applications namespace to reduce memory
items.body:
## Summary
- Scope the controller-runtime cache to the applications namespace (from `APPLICATIONS_NAMESPACE` env var) plus cluster-scoped resources, instead of watching all namespaces cluster-wide
- Use `DefaultTransform` with `StripUnusedFields` instead of per-type transforms
- Disable cache for ConfigMaps and Secrets (read fresh)

The operator was caching all Deployments, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, etc. across the entire cluster, consuming ~156Mi for a single-CR controller. With namespace scoping, memory usage should drop significantly.

The `APPLICATIONS_NAMESPACE` env var is injected by the ODH platform operator's `injectModuleEnv` action. When not set (standalone/dev), the cache falls back to cluster-wide (existing behavior).

Follows the pattern established by [ai-gateway-operator](https://github.com/opendatahub-io/ai-gateway-operator/blob/main/cmd/operator/operator.go#L99-L103).

## Test plan
- [ ] Deploy on cluster and verify memory usage drops
- [ ] Verify reconciliation works correctly with scoped cache
